templates.title: Idea Scorecard
howTo: List up to eight ideas in the Scorecard tab. One sentence each: what you sell and to whom.
Score each question 1 to 5. 1 = no, or no proof. 3 = maybe, some signs. 5 = yes, with proof you can point to.
Write the proof for question 1. No proof means the score can't go above 2. The sheet flags it.
Fill days to first sale and cost to start. They break ties.
Read the Decision tab. If two ideas are within 3 points, use the tie breakers in order.
Write your decision and the insider you'll talk to this week. Then stop scoring and start.
templates.summary: Score up to eight ideas against Eli's Idea Test in one sitting, see the winner, and use the tie breakers when two ideas are close.
templates.output: One idea chosen on purpose, with a score, the proof behind it and the insider you'll talk to this week.
templates.useWhen: Day 1 of the Start track, before you talk to a single customer.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that the winning idea names a specific customer, that every score of 3 or more has real proof written next to it, that the tie breakers were used when scores were close, and that an insider is named with a day this week.

roadmap.label: Start week 1, step 1: Score your ideas with the Idea Test

templates.title: Conversation Tracker
howTo: List 20 people who have the problem. Message 20 to get 10 conversations.
Pick where you found each one. Mix sources: DMs, Reddit, campus, family friends, local businesses.
Log the date you message them. The sheet sets a polite follow-up date three days later.
Update Status as you go. Booked and Interviewed rows count toward your goal of 10.
Right after each call, fill the grey-free columns: how they solve it today, what they pay, pain, and one exact quote.
Ask everyone: who else do you know who deals with this? Log referrals as new rows.
At 10 interviews, move to the Interview Synthesis sheet to make the call.
templates.summary: Track the 20 people you message to land 10 real customer conversations, with follow-up dates and the facts that matter from each call.
templates.output: Ten finished conversations logged in one place, with what each person pays today and their exact words.
templates.useWhen: Week 1 of the Start track, the moment you list the 10 people who have the problem.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that the people listed actually have the problem (not just friends being nice), that each finished interview records how they solve it today and what it costs them, and that the exact quotes are the customer's words rather than the member's summary.

templates.title: Interview Synthesis
howTo: In Interviews, give each conversation one row. Fill it from your notes, using their words.
In Phrases, paste any phrase that sounds like it could be a headline. Mark an x under every interview where you heard it.
Phrases heard 3 or more times turn lilac. Those are your headline, offer and ad words.
Open Verdict. The sheet suggests kill, pause or double down from your evidence.
Make your own call, write why, and if it's a pause, the one thing you'll change.
Double down? Take your top phrases into the One-Page Offer this week.
templates.summary: Lay your interviews side by side, count the phrases people repeat, and get a kill, pause or double down call backed by evidence.
templates.output: Your top repeated phrases in customers' exact words, what they pay today, and a written verdict.
templates.useWhen: Week 2 of the Start track after your interviews, and again in Grow when you rewrite your headline.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that the phrases are customers' exact words rather than the member's paraphrase, that the verdict follows the evidence (people paying today, recent pain, repeated words), and that a pause verdict names the one thing that will change.

templates.title: First-Sale Math
howTo: Open the Math tab. Fill the white cells for your test price in column B.
Add every cost one sale creates: supplies, packaging, shipping, platform and payment fees.
Look up your payment processor's current fees and enter them. Don't guess.
Enter the hours one sale takes you, start to finish, including messages.
Try a lower and a higher price in columns C and D to compare.
If one sale loses money, fix that before you spend a dollar on growth.
templates.summary: Check that one sale makes you money after every cost, what you really earn per hour, and how many sales cover your startup costs.
templates.output: Profit per sale, your real hourly rate and the number of sales you need, for three test prices side by side.
templates.useWhen: Week 3 of the Start track when you check the numbers can work, and before you set your price.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that every real cost per sale is included (materials, fees, shipping, time), that payment fees are entered from the processor's current pricing rather than guessed, that profit per sale is positive at the chosen price, and that the member is not relying on wishful volume.

roadmap.label: Start week 3, step 2: Check that the numbers can work

templates.title: Pricing Lab
howTo: Competitors: set a 30-minute timer. Log five competitors with price, model, what's included and what's missing.
Value: put a monthly number on the result you deliver. Extra customers, hours saved, money saved.
Price: enter your price. The sheet shows the ROI multiple, price per day and where you sit against competitors.
Copy the two framing lines into your One-Page Offer.
Test: offer the price to five real buyers. Say it plainly, then stop talking. Log every answer.
Five instant yeses? You're probably too cheap. Zero? Check the offer and the customer before you drop the price.
templates.summary: Research five competitors in 30 minutes, tie your price to the value you create, frame it small and large, and test it with five real buyers.
templates.output: A price you can defend, a one-line ROI story, both framings, and real yes or no answers from five buyers.
templates.useWhen: Week 1 of the Build track when you check pricing and margins, or any time you raise prices.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that the value estimate is believable and tied to a real customer outcome, that the price sits sensibly against the competitor range, that the framings use the smallest number for cost and the largest for value, and that the five-buyer test has real names and outcomes.

templates.title: Tool Stack Audit
howTo: List every tool you use or pay for, even free ones. Check your app store subscriptions and card statement.
Give each tool its one job. Enter the monthly cost and the last day you used it.
The sheet flags tools you haven't used in 14 days and jobs with two tools.
Mark each one Keep, Cut or Later. Later tools need a trigger: the pain that means you need it.
Open the Summary tab. Every core job should show one tool. Cancel what you cut today.
Rule: don't add a new tool until a task has hurt three times.
templates.summary: List every tool you pay for or log into, give each one job, and cut what you haven't used in two weeks, aiming for $0 to $50 a month.
templates.output: One tool per job for the six jobs every first business needs, your real monthly cost, and a cut list.
templates.useWhen: Week 2 of the Build track when you trim your tools, and any time a new app tempts you.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that there is exactly one kept tool per core job, that the kept monthly cost is near $0 to $50, that unused tools are cut, and that every 'later' tool names the pain that would justify it.

templates.title: Launch Countdown
howTo: Check items off here in the Library, or download the PDF or Word version.
Work top to bottom. Each group has a do-by date.
Ask Eli's Playbook to check anything you're unsure about.

items.text: Pick a launch date about 14 days out and put it on your calendar.
Text three people the date and ask them to check in on you.
Copy this countdown into Google Sheets, Notion or your notes app.

checklist.title: Two weeks before: set up the foundation

items.text: Finish your One-Page Offer.
Fill in your Landing Page Brief and build the page.
Run the five-point pre-launch check on your phone.
Set up payments: Shopify Payments for a store, or a payment link for a service.
Make a real payment with your own card, then refund it.
Look into registering your business. Check your local rules or ask a professional. This isn't legal or tax advice.
Set up a separate way to track business money. See Before You Take Money.
Write your delivery steps: everything that happens after someone pays.
Do one full test delivery with a friend.

checklist.title: One week before: warm up your list

items.text: Write your warm list in the Pipeline Tracker. Aim for 30 names.
Mark the 10 people most likely to buy.
Send those 10 a personal heads-up and ask if you can send them the link first.
Post once about what you're building and why.
Draft your launch post, your launch DM and your launch story.
Write the welcome message every new customer gets.
Write your three feedback questions.
Open the Objection Log so you can capture every "but" during launch week.
Send personal DMs to your top 10. One at a time, never a group message.
Post your launch post and your story.
Reply to every comment and DM the same day.
Log every reply and sale in the Pipeline Tracker.
Message the next 20 people on your warm list.
Ask your day 1 buyers if they know one person who'd want this.
Post something useful about the problem you solve, like a before and after or a quick tip.
Log every objection you've heard so far in the Objection Log.
Send one short, friendly follow-up to every maybe and every no-reply.
Deliver to your first customers with extra care. Over-deliver on the first orders.
Post a real update: what happened and what you learned.
Share a customer result only with their permission.
Count messages sent, replies, sales and objections.
Write down the one thing you'll change next week.

checklist.title: The week after: ask, learn, decide

items.text: Thank every customer within three days of delivery.
Ask every customer: What almost stopped you from buying? What was the best part? What would you change?
Ask happy customers if you can share their words or a photo. Use only what they approve.
Ask every non-buyer: What would have made it a yes?
Update your FAQ and landing page from the Objection Log.
Find the message, post or person that drove the most sales, and ask why it worked.
Pick one thing to do more of next week.
Set up simple revenue and expense tracking, and ask a professional about taxes where you live.

templates.summary: Every step from picking a launch date to the week after launch, with a do-by date for each so nothing important gets missed.
templates.output: A launch date on your calendar, a checked-off countdown and your first real numbers, from who you asked to who bought and what stopped the rest.
templates.useWhen: Build track week 3, about 14 days before you start asking people to pay, and every day through launch week.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that the launch date is about two weeks out, that payments were tested with a real purchase and refund, that registration is flagged for local rules or a professional, that the warm list has real names, and that the week-after questions ask what almost stopped people from buying.

templates.title: Before You Take Money
howTo: Check items off here in the Library, or download the PDF or Word version.
Work top to bottom. Each group has a do-by date.
Ask Eli's Playbook to check anything you're unsure about.

items.text: Pick one processor for what you sell: Shopify for a store, a payment link for a service, a card reader in person.
Check current fees and payout timing on the processor's own site.
Connect the account your payouts will go to.
Make a real payment with your own card.
Refund that payment and confirm the refund went through.
Turn on alerts so you know when money comes in.
Read each processor's current age rules before you sign up.
Ask a parent or guardian to open the account, or be added as its owner, if the rules require it.
Agree together on who can see the account and where payouts land.
Ask the same age question about any bank account for business money.
Ask a professional whether being under 18 changes anything else for you.
Never fake your age or use someone else's details to get around the rules.
Ask a professional which setup fits you, like a separate account or a business account.
Send every business payment to that one place.
Pay business costs from there, and never personal ones.
Store your logins in a password manager.
Make a simple sheet: date, what, sale or expense, amount, receipt link.
Log every sale and every expense the day it happens, even small ones.
Make one receipts folder and save a photo of every receipt.
Check the sheet against your payment app once a week.
Ask: do I need to register this business where I live?
Ask: do I need to register my business name, and can I use it?
Ask: does what I sell need a permit or license?
Ask: do I need to collect sales tax, and on what?
Ask: how is this income taxed for me, and how much should I set aside?
Ask: which records should I keep, and for how long?
Write down each answer, who gave it and the date.
Test your delivery time on a real order before you promise it.
Write your refund or guarantee policy in two or three sentences.
Put that policy where buyers see it before they pay.
Write what happens after someone pays, step by step, starting with the confirmation message.
Decide how you'll handle a refund request before the first one comes in.
Collect only what you need to deliver: name, contact and order details.
Keep customer info in one private place, like your Pipeline Tracker, and never share or sell it.
Never store card numbers yourself. Your processor handles them.
Ask before you add anyone to an email list.
Get permission before you post a customer's photo or words.

templates.summary: Set up payments, separate business money, keep simple records and write down your promises before your first customer pays you.
templates.output: A tested way to get paid and refund, business money kept separate, a sales and expense log from day one, written promises and answers from a local professional.
templates.useWhen: About two weeks before launch, in Build track week 3, alongside the Launch Countdown and before you share a payment link.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that a real payment and refund were tested, business money is kept separate, every sale and expense has a place to be logged, registration and tax questions went to a local professional instead of being guessed, and every promise to customers has been tested.

roadmap.label: Build week 3, step 1: Work through the launch checklist

templates.title: Objection Log
howTo: Every time someone hesitates, add a row: their exact words, where you heard it and the type.
Note whether they bought anyway and what you said that helped.
Open the FAQ tab. The sheet counts each type so you can see the real pattern.
Write a plain, true answer for the top three. Use their words in the question.
Put those answers on your landing page FAQ and into saved replies. Mark them fixed.
Each objection is also a post: a myth and the truth, or a question you answer on camera.
templates.summary: Write down every "but" you hear in the words people used, see which objections come up most, and turn the top three into your FAQ.
templates.output: Your top objections ranked, an honest answer for each, and the fixes for your landing page and DMs.
templates.useWhen: Launch week of the Build track (log every objection you hear), then any time sales stall.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that objections are logged in the customer's exact words, that the most common types are answered plainly and truthfully, that no answer uses pressure or fake scarcity, and that the top answers made it onto the landing page.

templates.title: Hours Audit
howTo: Open last week's calendar, screen time, texts and notes. List every business task and the hours it took.
Tag each one. Only me: needs your judgment, face or relationships. Repeat: same way every time. Waste: didn't need doing.
For repeat tasks, answer: same steps every time? Fine if done 80% as well?
The sheet scores each repeat task. Highest score = your best first handoff.
Pick who or what runs it: a saved reply, an automation, an AI tool, a freelancer or a friend.
Cut every waste task today. Then write the SOP for your first handoff.
templates.summary: List every task from last week with the time it took, tag it only me, repeat or waste, and let the sheet pick your best first handoff.
templates.output: Last week's hours by tag, a cut list, your biggest bottleneck and the one task to hand off first.
templates.useWhen: Week 1 of the systems roadmap and once a month after, alongside the One-Page SOP.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that the audit lists real tasks with honest hours, that waste tasks are cut, that the first handoff is repeated, rule-based and low-risk rather than a judgment-heavy task, and that the chosen person or tool fits the task.

templates.title: Weekly Founder Scorecard
howTo: Each Monday, pull last week's numbers from the same places: platform analytics, site dashboard, DMs, payment app.
Type them into the next row of the Scorecard tab. Zero is a number. Enter it.
Add your inputs too: posts, messages sent, hours. When everything drops, check these first.
Read the grey columns: each conversion rate, the change from last week and the biggest drop.
Write one double down, one pause, one kill and the one test for next week.
Open This week for the summary and the Charts tab for the trend. One week is a data point. Three is a trend.
Want it emailed to you every Monday? Set up the Monday Scorecard Email recipe on this sheet.
templates.summary: Ten minutes every Monday: your five numbers, the conversion rate between each step, week-over-week change and one decision for next week.
templates.output: A 13-week scorecard that shows where your business leaks, what changed, and a written kill, pause or double down call.
templates.useWhen: The last week of the Build track, then every Monday, and in Grow week 4 to compare this week to week one.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that all five numbers are filled from the same sources each week, that the member found the step with the biggest drop rather than just the biggest number, that each week has one kill, one pause and one double down, and that the test for next week is specific.

templates.title: 30-Day Content Planner
howTo: Open Setup. Write your three pillars: one that teaches, one that shows proof, one that shows you.
Pick one main platform, your rhythm (5 or 3 days a week) and your Day 1 date. Every date and pillar fills in.
Block a two-hour batching slot on your calendar. Write it in Setup.
In Calendar, fill week one completely: hook, topic, format, CTA. Weeks two to four get topics only.
48 hours after each post, log views, saves and shares, comments and DMs.
Open Formats each week. Reuse the format that wins on DMs and comments, not just views.
Day 29: remake your best post a new way. Day 30: plan next month. Keep, cut, test.
templates.summary: Three pillars, one platform and a posting rhythm you can keep, laid out over 30 dated days, with a tracker that tells you which format hits.
templates.output: Week one fully planned, weeks two to four with topics, a batching slot, and a format you know is working by day 30.
templates.useWhen: Week 3 of the Build track, Week 2 of Grow, or any month you plan founder-led content.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that the three pillars are distinct and tied to the customer's problem, that one pillar features the member personally, that the rhythm is realistic for under three hours a week, that week one has a hook, topic, format and CTA for every post, and that results are logged 48 hours after posting.

templates.title: Hook Bank
howTo: Browse the Hook bank tab. Filter by type: story, mistake, contrarian, how-to, result, behind the scenes.
In My hooks, write ten hooks for your niche. Put the template number in the # column and the type fills in.
Say each hook out loud. If it sounds like an ad, rewrite it until it sounds like you.
After posting, log views, saves and DMs at 48 hours. The sheet compares each one to your average.
Open Results to see which hook type wins. Use at least two types each week so you have a comparison.
Review your winner in Winners and write three remixes: same winning element, new topic.
templates.summary: 42 fill-in-the-blank hooks, 10 caption templates and 10 calls to action, plus a log that shows which hook type works for your audience.
templates.output: Ten hooks written for your niche, the hook type that beats your average, and three remixes of your best post.

howTo: Check items off here in the Library, or download the PDF or Word version.
Work top to bottom. Each group has a do-by date.
Ask Eli's Playbook to check anything you're unsure about.

items.text: Put your two-hour slot on the calendar, same time every week.
Charge your phone and clear space for video.
Clean the camera lens.
Pick one spot with window light facing you.
Pull last week's comments and DMs for post ideas.
Open your three pillars and your Hook Bank, or a note of hooks you've saved.
Write five hooks, with at least one from each pillar.
Fill each hook's blanks with your customers' exact words.
Write a one-line outline under each hook.
Pick one format per post.
Fill in the shot list below.
Set the phone at eye level and lock focus.
Record a 10-second test and check the sound.
Film all five back to back in the same spot.
Start talking on the first frame. No warm-up.
Shoot each hook two or three ways.
Grab extra clips: hands at work, before and after, your setup.
Pick the best take of each hook.
Cut every pause and every 'um'.
Add auto captions and fix any wrong words.
Put the hook on screen in the first two seconds.
Keep each video under 45 seconds.
Watch each one on your phone with the sound off.
Write a short caption for each post.
Give each post one call to action: follow, comment or DM.
Schedule all five with the platform's own scheduler.
Check the days match your posting rhythm.
Log each post in your 30-Day Content Planner.
Reply to every comment within a day.
Write down every question people ask. That's next week's batch.
Fill in the format tracker 48 hours after each post.

templates.summary: Film a full week of short videos in one two-hour block: plan, film, edit and schedule five posts, with a shot list that keeps you on track.
templates.output: Five edited, captioned posts scheduled for the week, a filled shot list and a list of questions to answer in next week's batch.
templates.useWhen: Grow track week 2, once your three content pillars are set, then once a week in the same slot.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that the five hooks cover all three pillars and use the customer's words, each post has one format and one call to action, videos stay under 45 seconds with the hook on screen in the first two seconds, and all five are scheduled and logged.

roadmap.label: Grow week 2, step 3: Batch-create one full week of posts

templates.title: Landing Page Leak Audit
howTo: Check items off here in the Library, or download the PDF or Word version.
Work top to bottom. Each group has a do-by date.
Ask Eli's Playbook to check anything you're unsure about.

items.text: Show the page to a stranger for five seconds, then ask what you sell and who it's for.
Make the headline the result customers want, in their words.
Make the subhead say who it's for and how it works.
Open the page on your phone.
Check the button shows without scrolling.
Check every block reads cleanly, with nothing cut off.
Load it on mobile data. If you're waiting, shrink or cut images.
List exactly what they get.
Frame the price as the smallest true number, like per week or per session.
Offer only a guarantee you can honor every time.
Promise only a delivery time you've already tested.
Show only real proof: conversations, photos of real work, pilot results, your story.
Delete any number, review or logo you can't back up.
Get permission for every customer quote and photo.
Pull your top three objections from your Objection Log or your DMs.
Answer all three plainly on the page.
Use one call to action: one button, one next step.
Repeat that same button at the top and the bottom.
Tap every button and link on your phone.
Complete a real purchase or booking, then refund or cancel it.
Check the buyer gets a confirmation message right away.
Check you get notified of every sale, booking or form.
Write down this week's visits and leads from your Weekly Founder Scorecard.
Work out visits to leads (leads divided by visits). That's your before number.

templates.summary: Run 24 quick checks on a page people visit but don't buy from, find the three biggest leaks and fix them one at a time.
templates.output: Your page checked on a phone, your top three leaks with a fix for each, and a before-and-after number that shows whether each fix worked.
templates.useWhen: Grow track week 3, or any week your Weekly Founder Scorecard shows visits going up while leads stay flat.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that the five-second test was done with a real stranger, all proof is real, there is exactly one call to action, checkout or booking was tested end to end, and each leak has one fix, a date and a before-and-after number.

roadmap.label: Grow week 3, step 2: Fix the biggest leak on your sales page

templates.title: Ad Test Planner
howTo: Answer the five readiness checks in Plan. Fewer than three yes? Skip paid for now and go back to outreach and content.
Enter the most you can lose without stress. That's your cap, for one test, not per month.
Enter a cautious guess for cost per click, your page's conversion rate and your price.
Read the expected visitors, sales and cost per sale. Write your stop rule before you launch the ad.
Each day of the test, log spend, clicks, visits and sales in Daily log.
When the sheet says stop, stop. Change one thing only, then run the next test with the same cap.
templates.summary: Plan a small, capped paid test, write your stop rule before you spend a dollar, then log each day so the sheet tells you when to stop.
templates.output: A test cap, an expected cost per sale, a stop rule written in advance, and a daily log that flags when you hit it.
templates.useWhen: Week 3 of the Grow track, only after free channels show signal, real conversations and a page that converts warm traffic.
templates.aiPrompt: Check that the test cap is an amount the member can lose without stress, that organic signal exists before paid spend, that the stop rule was set before the test and follows the two-sales rule, and that doubling down is tied to cost per sale versus what a sale earns. Nothing here is financial advice.
